note:

rejected.title: Using economic indicators as evidence
card: An economic indicator is a figure that measures part of the economy. The unemployment rate measures jobs, and the inflation rate measures how fast prices rise. A claim about the economy is stronger when a figure backs it.

A figure only supports a claim if it matches the claim: what it measures, the area it covers and the period. A claim about a whole town over the last year needs figures for the whole town over the last year.
Check the source. Figures from a statistics agency or a government body are usually collected by set methods. A figure with no named source is hard to trust.
One figure rarely tells the whole story. Using two or more indicators gives a fuller picture than one.
rejected.remember: Good evidence is a figure that fits the claim, covers the right period and comes from a clear source.

a.q: Which choice best uses an indicator as evidence for the claim that prices rose faster in 2023 than in 2020?
opts: Inflation rates for both years from a statistics agency
A news headline saying that prices feel very high these days
The unemployment rate for 2023 from a government report
Inflation for 2023 only, from a post with no named source
a.why: The claim compares prices in two years, so it needs inflation figures for both years from a clear source. The unemployment rate is a figure, but it measures jobs, not prices, so it does not match the claim.
a.clue: Match the figure to the claim, the years and the source.

b.q: Priya says her town's economy is growing strongly. She quotes a small business owner's sales figures from last month. Why is this weak evidence?
opts: It covers one business and one month, not the whole town
It is a recent figure, and older figures are more reliable
It is about sales, and inflation is what shows growth
It is a number, and a claim needs a quote from an expert
b.why: The claim is about the whole town economy, but the figure covers one business over one short period, so it does not match the claim. Recent figures are not the problem, and inflation measures prices, not growth.
b.clue: Ask what the figure covers and what the claim covers.

A figure supports a claim when it matches what the claim is about, the area it covers and the period. Check the source too: figures from a statistics agency or government body are collected by set methods, and a figure with no named source is hard to trust.
One figure rarely tells the whole story. Using two or more indicators gives a fuller picture, and a claim backed by matching figures is stronger.
final.remember: Good evidence is a figure that fits the claim, covers the right period and comes from a clear source.

a.q: Which evidence best supports the claim that prices rose faster in 2023 than in 2020?
opts: Inflation rates for both years from a statistics agency
A news headline saying that prices feel very high these days
The unemployment rate for 2023 from a government report
Inflation for 2023 alone, from a post with no named source
a.why: The claim compares prices in two years, so it needs inflation figures for both years from a clear source. The unemployment rate is a figure, but it measures the share of the labour force (people working or looking for work) who have no job, not prices, so it does not match the claim.
a.clue: Match the figure to the claim, the years and the source.

b.q: Priya claims her town's economy is growing strongly. As proof, she quotes one café owner's sales for last month. Why is this weak evidence?
opts: It covers one business and one month, not the whole town
It is a recent figure, and older figures are more reliable
It is about sales, and inflation is what shows growth
It is a number, and a claim needs a quote from an expert
b.why: The claim is about the whole town's economy, but the figure covers one business over one short period, so it does not match the claim. Recent figures are not the problem, and inflation measures how fast prices rise, not growth.
b.clue: Ask what the figure covers and what the claim covers.
